key_terms.meaning: v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ); fixed completely by peak V<sub>m</sub>, angular frequency ω = 2πf, and phase φ
V<sub>m</sub>, the largest instantaneous value a sine wave reaches; units volts or amperes
The steady DC value that heats a resistor equally; for a pure sine V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 0.707 V<sub>m</sub>
Over one full cycle of a sine it is zero; over a half cycle it is (2/π)V<sub>m</sub> = 0.637 V<sub>m</sub>
RMS divided by half-cycle average; for a pure sine k = 1.11
φ in ωt + φ; the shift in radians or degrees between two sinusoids of the same frequency
ω = 2πf rad/s, where f is the frequency in hertz
A complex number V = V<sub>rms</sub>∠φ that holds the amplitude and phase of a sinusoid at one fixed ω
Z = V/I = R + jX in ohms; carries both the magnitude ratio and the phase shift
The imaginary part of Z: X<sub>L</sub> = ωL and X<sub>C</sub> = −1/(ωC), both in ohms
Y = 1/Z = G + jB in siemens; series and parallel combine with the opposite rules to Z
The frequency ω₀ = 1/√(LC) at which X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, so the net reactance X<sub>L</sub> − X<sub>C</sub> is zero and a series circuit's impedance is purely R
S = V I* = P + jQ in volt-amperes; its magnitude is the apparent power
P = VI cos φ in watts; the part that does useful work and cannot be recovered
Q = VI sin φ in volt-amperes reactive (var); the part that swings between source and reactance
cos φ, the ratio of real power to apparent power; lagging when current lags voltage (inductive)
The order in which the three phase voltages reach their peaks, for example R–Y–B
The phasor sum I<sub>R</sub> + I<sub>Y</sub> + I<sub>B</sub>; zero for a balanced load, non-zero when unbalanced
In star, V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>; in delta, V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub>

Two wattmeters in any two lines of a three-wire system; total power = W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> for any load, and tan φ = √3(W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub>)/(W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub>) for a balanced load
A component at an integer multiple nω of the fundamental frequency, arising from a non-sinusoidal wave
The expansion of a periodic wave as a DC term plus a sum of sine and cosine harmonics
THD = √(V₂² + V₃² + …)/V₁, the RMS of all harmonics divided by the fundamental
For harmonics, RMS total = √(V₀² + V₁² + V₂² + …); powers add, voltages do not

takeaways: A sinusoid is fully described by three numbers — peak, frequency and phase — and for a pure sine the heating value is the peak divided by √2.
At one fixed frequency a phasor replaces the whole time function, so adding sinusoids becomes adding complex numbers.
Impedance Z = R + jX lets every DC rule (series, parallel, mesh, nodal, Thevenin) work unchanged, provided you keep the j.
In an AC steady-state solution the answer is the forced (particular) solution; the switching transient has already died out.
Complex power S = P + jQ separates the useful watts from the reactive vars, and the power factor is the cosine of the angle between them.
A balanced three-phase supply delivers constant total power at every instant and cancels in the neutral, so one phase can be solved alone.
An unbalanced star load needs its neutral: without it the star point shifts and the lightly loaded phases see more than the phase voltage.
Two wattmeters in any two lines of a three-wire system give the total power for any load; for a balanced load the same two readings also give the reactive power and the power factor.
A non-sinusoidal periodic wave breaks into harmonics, and each harmonic is solved as its own AC problem before the RMS values combine root-sum-square.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to set up the circuit in phasor or complex form, show the algebra with units, and then interpret the result physically — power factor, phase angle, wattmeter readings or harmonic content — rather than stopping at a number.

bank.q: Define peak value, RMS value, average value and form factor for a periodic waveform. Derive the RMS and half-cycle average values of a pure sine wave and hence show that its form factor is 1.11.
outline: State the definition of RMS as the square root of the mean of the square over one period.
Square the sine, use sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2, integrate over one period, divide by the period.
Result V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 0.707 V<sub>m</sub>.
Half-cycle average = (2/π)V<sub>m</sub> = 0.637 V<sub>m</sub>; full-cycle average of a sine is zero.
Form factor k = 0.707/0.637 = 1.11; k ≥ 1 for every waveform, and k = 1 only when |v| is constant, as for DC or a square wave
answer: Definitions. The peak value V<sub>m</sub> is the largest instantaneous value. The average value is the signed area under the wave over an interval divided by that interval; for a wave that is symmetric about the axis it is taken over one half cycle, because the full-cycle average is zero. The RMS (effective) value is the square root of the mean of v² over one period: the DC voltage that heats a resistor equally. The form factor is V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>avg</sub>; the peak factor is V<sub>m</sub>/V<sub>rms</sub>.

answer.text: RMS of v = V<sub>m</sub> sin θ, with θ = ωt and one period 2π:
answer.pre:
V<sub>rms</sub>² = (1/2π) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> V<sub>m</sub>² sin²θ dθ
        = (V<sub>m</sub>²/2π) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> (1 − cos 2θ)/2 dθ
        = (V<sub>m</sub>²/2π) [θ/2 − (sin 2θ)/4]<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup>
        = (V<sub>m</sub>²/2π) × π = V<sub>m</sub>²/2
V<sub>rms</sub>  = V<sub>m</sub>/√2 = 0.707 V<sub>m</sub>

answer: The cos 2θ term runs through two whole cycles in 0 to 2π, so its integral is zero; only the constant ½ survives. That is why the mean of sin² is exactly ½.

answer.pre:
V<sub>avg</sub> = (1/π) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> V<sub>m</sub> sin θ dθ = (V<sub>m</sub>/π) [−cos θ]<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup>
      = (V<sub>m</sub>/π)(1 + 1) = 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 0.637 V<sub>m</sub>
Full cycle: (1/2π) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> V<sub>m</sub> sin θ dθ = 0

answer: Form factor: (V<sub>m</sub>/√2) ÷ (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) = π/(2√2) = 1.111. Peak factor: V<sub>m</sub> ÷ (V<sub>m</sub>/√2) = √2 = 1.414. Both are pure numbers, so they describe the shape of the wave and not its size.

What the number means: a form factor above 1 says the wave is peaky. A square wave, flat at ±V<sub>m</sub>, has RMS = average = V<sub>m</sub> and form factor 1.00; a triangle has 0.577/0.500 = 1.155; the sine sits between at 1.11. An average-reading meter multiplies the average by 1.11, so it is right only for a sine.
Check with the mains: 230 V RMS gives V<sub>m</sub> = 230 × 1.414 = 325.3 V and V<sub>avg</sub> = 0.637 × 325.3 = 207.1 V. Then 230/207.1 = 1.11 and 325.3/230 = 1.414, as derived.

bank.q: Explain the phasor concept. Why can a sinusoid be represented by a complex number only when the frequency is fixed? Draw the phasor diagrams for a pure resistor, a pure inductor and a pure capacitor.
outline: A phasor is a rotating vector frozen at t = 0; its length is the RMS (or peak) value and its angle is the phase.
The e<sup>jωt</sup> factor is common to every signal in the circuit, so it can be dropped and restored at the end.
Different frequencies would rotate at different rates, so a single frozen snapshot would be meaningless.
Resistor: V and I in phase. Inductor: I lags V by 90°. Capacitor: I leads V by 90°.
State the corresponding impedances R, jωL and 1/(jωC).
answer: A sinusoid v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> cos(ωt + φ) is the real part of V<sub>m</sub>e<sup>jφ</sup>e<sup>jωt</sup>: a vector of length V<sub>m</sub> that starts at angle φ and turns anticlockwise at ω rad/s. Its projection on the real axis traces v(t).

The phasor is that rotating vector frozen at t = 0: V = V<sub>m</sub>∠φ (or V<sub>m</sub>/√2∠φ for an RMS phasor). It keeps the two numbers that change from point to point in a circuit, magnitude and phase, and drops the factor e<sup>jωt</sup>.

Why the frequency must be fixed: dropping e<sup>jωt</sup> is allowed only when every voltage and current carries the same factor, so it cancels from every KVL and KCL equation. In a linear circuit driven at one frequency this is true in the steady state. Two waves at different frequencies turn at different rates, so the angle between them keeps changing: 10∠0° at 50 Hz and 5∠0° at 150 Hz are in phase at t = 0 but not 1 ms later, and their sum is not a sinusoid at all. One frozen picture cannot describe them.

Differentiation becomes multiplication by jω, because d/dt e<sup>jωt</sup> = jω e<sup>jωt</sup>. So v = L di/dt becomes V = jωL I and i = C dv/dt becomes I = jωC V: the differential equations of the circuit become algebra.
Resistor: v = Ri gives V = R I, a real factor, so V and I are in phase. With R = 10 Ω and I = 2∠0° A, V = 20∠0° V.
Inductor: V = jωL I. With L = 31.8 mH at 50 Hz, ωL = 10 Ω and V = j10 × 2∠0° = 20∠90° V: the voltage leads the current by 90° (the current lags).
Capacitor: V = I/(jωC) = −j I/(ωC). With C = 318 µF at 50 Hz, 1/(ωC) = 10 Ω and V = −j10 × 2∠0° = 20∠−90° V: the voltage lags the current by 90° (the current leads).

bank.q: Define real power, reactive power, apparent power and complex power. Draw the power triangle and explain the meaning of the power factor.
outline: P = VI cos φ in watts; Q = VI sin φ in var; |S| = VI in VA.
S = V I* = P + jQ; P is the average of the instantaneous power, Q has zero average.
Power triangle: P along the horizontal, Q vertical, S the hypotenuse, φ the angle.
Power factor = cos φ = P/|S|; lagging for inductive, leading for capacitive loads.
Reactive power is not consumed; it oscillates between source and reactance.
answer: Start from p(t) = v(t) i(t) with v = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt) and i = I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt − φ). Using sin A sin B = ½[cos(A − B) − cos(A + B)]: p(t) = V I cos φ − V I cos(2ωt − φ), with V and I the RMS values.

Real (active) power P is the average of p(t). The double-frequency term averages to zero, so P = V I cos φ, in watts (W). It is the power turned into heat, light or shaft work, and only resistance absorbs it: P = I²R.

Reactive power Q = V I sin φ, in volt-ampere reactive (var). It is the peak rate at which energy flows into the inductance or capacitance and back each half cycle; its average is zero. By the usual convention Q > 0 for an inductive (lagging) load and Q < 0 for a capacitive (leading) load.
Apparent power |S| = V I, in volt-amperes (VA): the product of the two meter readings. It fixes the current, so it sets the size of cables, transformers and generators.
Complex power S = V I* = P + jQ, where I* is the conjugate of the current phasor. With V = V∠0° and I = I∠−φ, S = V I∠φ = V I cos φ + jV I sin φ.

answer.text: Power triangle for a motor taking 10 A from 230 V at 0.8 pf lagging: |S| = 2300 VA, P = 2300 × 0.8 = 1840 W, Q = 2300 × 0.6 = 1380 var.

svg.aria: Power triangle: real power 1840 W along the base, reactive power 1380 var upward, apparent power 2300 VA along the hypotenuse, angle 36.87 degrees.

answer: Power factor = cos φ = P/|S|, the fraction of the volt-amperes that does work. It is lagging when the current lags (inductive) and leading when it leads (capacitive). For the motor it is 1840/2300 = 0.8. A low power factor means more current for the same watts, hence bigger I²R loss and voltage drop, which is why supply tariffs penalise it.
Check: √(1840² + 1380²) = √(3 385 600 + 1 904 400) = √5 290 000 = 2300 VA, so the three sides close the triangle.

bank.q: For a balanced star-connected three-phase supply, derive the relations between line and phase voltages and between line and phase currents. Show that the neutral current is zero for a balanced load.
outline: Phase voltages are equal in magnitude and 120° apart: V<sub>R</sub> = V∠0°, V<sub>Y</sub> = V∠−120°, V<sub>B</sub> = V∠+120°.
Line voltage V<sub>RY</sub> = V<sub>R</sub> − V<sub>Y</sub>; using phasor subtraction its magnitude is √3 V<sub>ph</sub> and it leads V<sub>R</sub> by 30°.
In star I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>, so each line carries the phase current.
Phasor sum of the three equal currents 120° apart is zero, so no neutral current flows.
Instantaneous total power is constant at 3 V<sub>ph</sub> I<sub>ph</sub> cos φ.
answer: Take R-Y-B (positive) sequence with V<sub>R</sub> as reference: V<sub>R</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>∠0°, V<sub>Y</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>∠−120°, V<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>∠120°, all RMS line-to-neutral voltages.

answer.text: Line voltage between R and Y, by KVL around R, neutral and Y:
answer.pre:
V<sub>RY</sub> = V<sub>R</sub> − V<sub>Y</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>∠0° − V<sub>ph</sub>∠−120°
     = V<sub>ph</sub>[1 − (−0.5 − j0.866)] = V<sub>ph</sub>(1.5 + j0.866)
|V<sub>RY</sub>| = V<sub>ph</sub>√(1.5² + 0.866²) = V<sub>ph</sub>√3,  angle = tan⁻¹(0.866/1.5) = 30°
V<sub>RY</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub>∠30°

answer: In the same way V<sub>YB</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub>∠−90° and V<sub>BR</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub>∠150°: the three line voltages are equal, 120° apart, and each leads its phase voltage by 30°. So V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub>; for 230.9 V phase, V<sub>L</sub> = 400 V.
Currents: in a star each line conductor is in series with one phase winding, so the same current flows in both: I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>, with no phase shift.

answer.text: Neutral current for a balanced load Z = |Z|∠φ in every phase. Each current is I<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>/|Z| at its own phase angle minus φ:

answer: So a balanced four-wire star needs no neutral current, which is why a balanced load can be solved one phase at a time.

Total power: each phase gives p<sub>k</sub>(t) = V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub>[cos φ − cos(2ωt − φ − 2θ<sub>k</sub>)] with θ<sub>k</sub> = 0°, −120°, 120°. The three double-frequency terms are 240° apart, so they also add to zero, and p(t) = 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub> cos φ at every instant: a three-phase motor gets a smooth torque.

Check with numbers: Z = 10 + j6 Ω on 400 V. V<sub>ph</sub> = 230.9 V, I<sub>ph</sub> = I<sub>L</sub> = 230.9/11.66 = 19.80 A at −30.96°, −150.96° and 89.04°; their sum is zero, and P = 3 × 19.80² × 10 = 11.76 kW = √3 × 400 × 19.80 × 0.857.

bank.q: A coil of resistance 8 Ω and inductance 30 mH is connected in series with a 100 μF capacitor across a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find the impedance, the current, the voltage across each element, and the power factor.
outline: X<sub>L</sub> = ωL = 9.42 Ω, X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(ωC) = 31.83 Ω, net X = −22.41 Ω
Z = 8 − j22.41 Ω, |Z| = 23.79 Ω, angle −70.35° (capacitive)
I = 230/23.79 = 9.67 A, leading the voltage by 70.35°
V<sub>R</sub> = 77.3 V, V<sub>L</sub> = 91.1 V, V<sub>C</sub> = 307.7 V, coil voltage 119.5 V; V<sub>C</sub> exceeds the supply, so check by phasor sum
Power factor = cos 70.35° = 0.336 leading; P = I²R = 748 W
answer: Net reactance X = X<sub>L</sub> − X<sub>C</sub> = 9.42 − 31.83 = −22.41 Ω. It is negative, so the circuit is capacitive.
Current, with the supply as reference V = 230∠0° V: I = 230∠0°/23.79∠−70.35° = 9.67∠70.35° A. It leads the supply by 70.35°.
The capacitor voltage, 307.7 V, is larger than the supply. That is possible because V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are 180° apart: their net is 91.1 − 307.7 = −216.6 V along the reactive axis.
Phasor check: |V| = √(77.3² + 216.6²) = √(5975 + 46 916) = √52 891 = 229.98 V ≈ 230 V. The parts rebuild the supply.
Power factor = cos 70.35° = 0.336 leading. Real power P = I²R = 9.667² × 8 = 747.7 W, which equals V I cos θ = 230 × 9.667 × 0.336 = 747.7 W. Reactive power Q = V I sin θ = −2094 var (capacitive).

bank.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 15 Ω resistor in parallel with a 0.1 H inductor. Find the admittance, the total current, the real and reactive power drawn, and the power factor.
outline: Branch admittances: G = 1/15 = 0.0667 S; Y<sub>L</sub> = 1/(j31.42) = −j0.0318 S
I = V Y = 16.99 A at −25.5°, so the current lags
P = V²G = 3527 W; Q = V²/X<sub>L</sub> = +1684 var (positive, because the load is inductive)
Power factor cos 25.5° = 0.902 lagging; |S| = 3908 VA
answer: The voltage is common to the two branches, so work with admittances. X<sub>L</sub> = ωL = 314.16 × 0.1 = 31.42 Ω.
Branch admittances: G = 1/15 = 0.0667 S; Y<sub>L</sub> = 1/(j31.42) = −j0.0318 S.
KCL check: 15.33 − j7.32 has magnitude √(235.1 + 53.6) = 16.99 A, the same as V|Y|.
Real power: only the resistor takes it. P = V²G = 230²/15 = 3527 W.
Reactive power: Q = V²/X<sub>L</sub> = 230²/31.42 = 1684 var, positive because the load is inductive. (In admittance form Q = −V²B with B = −0.0318 S, which also gives +1684 var.)
Apparent power |S| = V I = 230 × 16.99 = 3908 VA; check √(3527² + 1684²) = 3908 VA. Power factor = P/|S| = 3527/3908 = 0.902 lagging, equal to cos 25.52°.

bank.q: In a three-phase, three-wire system the two wattmeters read W₁ = 8 kW and W₂ = 2 kW. Find the total power, the power factor and the reactive power. State what happens when the load power factor falls to 0.5.
outline: Total power P = W₁ + W₂ = 10 kW.
Power factor = cos 46.1° = 0.693 lagging.
Q = √3 (W₁ − W₂) = 10.39 kvar; alternatively Q = P tan φ.
At pf 0.5, φ = 60° and one wattmeter reads zero; below 0.5 that wattmeter reads negative and its connection must be reversed.
answer: Total real power: P = W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> = 8 + 2 = 10 kW. This holds for any load on three wires.

For a balanced lagging load W<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° − φ) and W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° + φ), so tan φ = √3(W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub>)/(W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub>).
Power factor = cos 46.10° = 0.693 lagging.
Reactive power Q = √3(W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub>) = 1.732 × 6 = 10.39 kvar. Check: Q = P tan φ = 10 × 1.039 = 10.39 kvar. Apparent power |S| = P/pf = 10/0.693 = 14.42 kVA.
Back-check of the readings: V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> = |S|/√3 = 8.33 kVA. W<sub>1</sub> = 8.33 cos(−16.10°) = 8.00 kW and W<sub>2</sub> = 8.33 cos 76.10° = 2.00 kW, the given readings.
When the power factor falls to 0.5: φ = 60°, so W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos 90° = 0 and the whole power shows on W<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(−30°).

Below 0.5 lagging, 30° + φ passes 90°, so W<sub>2</sub> is negative and the pointer kicks backwards. Reverse its voltage-coil (or current-coil) connection to read it, and enter the reading as negative: P = W<sub>1</sub> − |W<sub>2</sub>|. At pf = 0.3, for example, φ = 72.5° and W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos 102.5° = −0.216 V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>.

bank.q: A square wave of peak amplitude 100 V alternates between +100 V and −100 V with a 50% duty cycle. Write its Fourier series, find its RMS value from the series, and compare it with the direct RMS.
outline: No DC term; only odd sine harmonics: v(t) = (4V<sub>m</sub>/π)[sin ωt + (1/3)sin 3ωt + (1/5)sin 5ωt + …].
Peak of the nth harmonic = 4V<sub>m</sub>/(nπ) for odd n.
RMS = √(V₁² + V₃² + V₅² + …) with each V<sub>n</sub> = peak/√2; the sum of 1/n² over odd n gives π²/8.
Result equals V<sub>m</sub> = 100 V, the same as the direct RMS of a square wave.
Form factor of a square wave is 1.0; compare with 1.11 for a sine.
answer: Take v(t) = +V<sub>m</sub> for 0 < θ < π and −V<sub>m</sub> for π < θ < 2π, with θ = ωt and V<sub>m</sub> = 100 V. It is an odd function and has half-wave symmetry, so the DC term and every a<sub>n</sub> are zero and only odd n survive.

answer.pre:
b<sub>n</sub> = (1/π) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> v sin nθ dθ = (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> sin nθ dθ
    = (2V<sub>m</sub>/nπ)(1 − cos nπ)
    = 4V<sub>m</sub>/(nπ) for odd n,  0 for even n

answer: Series: v(t) = (4V<sub>m</sub>/π)[sin ωt + (1/3) sin 3ωt + (1/5) sin 5ωt + …] = 127.3 sin ωt + 42.4 sin 3ωt + 25.5 sin 5ωt + … V.

answer.text: RMS from the series: each harmonic has RMS = peak/√2, and the RMS values combine as a root-sum-square.

answer: All the terms: V<sub>rms</sub>² = Σ (4V<sub>m</sub>/nπ)²/2 over odd n = (8V<sub>m</sub>²/π²)(1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + …) = (8V<sub>m</sub>²/π²)(π²/8) = V<sub>m</sub>². So V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> = 100 V. The partial sums in the table creep up towards it; six harmonics already give 98.3 V.
Direct RMS: v² = 100² = 10 000 V² at every instant, so its mean is 10 000 and V<sub>rms</sub> = 100 V. The two routes agree.
Average over a half cycle = 100 V, so the form factor is 100/100 = 1.00, against 1.11 for a sine: the square wave is as flat as a wave can be.
The THD of the square wave follows from the same numbers: √(100² − 90.03²)/90.03 = 43.53/90.03 = 0.483, that is 48.3 %, even though no single harmonic exceeds a third of the fundamental.

bank.q: A star-connected load with unequal impedances Z<sub>R</sub> = 10∠0° Ω, Z<sub>Y</sub> = 10∠−30° Ω, Z<sub>B</sub> = 10∠30° Ω is fed from a balanced 400 V, three-phase, four-wire supply. Find the line currents and the neutral current.
outline: Phase voltage = 400/√3 = 230.9 V
Neutral current I<sub>N</sub> = I<sub>R</sub> + I<sub>Y</sub> + I<sub>B</sub> = 23.09∠0° A: the Y and B currents cancel and the neutral carries a current as large as a line current
A broken neutral would shift the star point and change all three load voltages
answer: With a solid neutral each load phase is held at its own supply voltage, so each phase is solved on its own. V<sub>ph</sub> = 400/√3 = 230.9 V; with R-Y-B sequence V<sub>R</sub> = 230.9∠0°, V<sub>Y</sub> = 230.9∠−120°, V<sub>B</sub> = 230.9∠120° V.

answer.text: Line currents (I = V/Z, divide magnitudes and subtract angles):

answer: The three magnitudes are equal, but the load is still unbalanced: the angles are no longer 120° apart because the impedance angles differ.

Neutral current, the return from the load star point to the source: I<sub>N</sub> = I<sub>R</sub> + I<sub>Y</sub> + I<sub>B</sub> = 23.09 + (−j23.09) + (j23.09) = 23.09∠0° A. The Y and B currents cancel each other, and the neutral carries a current as large as a line current.

Power: P<sub>R</sub> = 23.09² × 10 = 5333 W; P<sub>Y</sub> = P<sub>B</sub> = 230.9 × 23.09 × cos 30° = 4619 W. Total P = 14 571 W. (Phase Y draws −2667 var and phase B +2667 var, so the total reactive power is zero.)

What the neutral does: it holds the load star point at the source neutral. If it broke, the three currents would be forced to sum to zero, the star point would shift, and the three load voltages would become unequal; some loads would get more than 230.9 V.
Check: KCL at the load star point gives I<sub>R</sub> + I<sub>Y</sub> + I<sub>B</sub> − I<sub>N</sub> = 23.09 − 23.09 = 0.

bank.q: Show that the two-wattmeter method gives the total power and the power-factor angle of a three-phase load whether the load is balanced or unbalanced. Derive tan φ = √3(W₁ − W₂)/(W₁ + W₂) for the balanced case and explain a negative reading.
outline: Current coils in lines R and Y, voltage coils from R to B and from Y to B

W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> = average of v<sub>RB</sub> i<sub>R</sub> + v<sub>YB</sub> i<sub>Y</sub>; since i<sub>R</sub> + i<sub>Y</sub> + i<sub>B</sub> = 0 this equals v<sub>R</sub> i<sub>R</sub> + v<sub>Y</sub> i<sub>Y</sub> + v<sub>B</sub> i<sub>B</sub>, the total power, for any load

Balanced load, R-Y-B sequence: the angle between V<sub>RB</sub> and I<sub>R</sub> is 30° − φ and between V<sub>YB</sub> and I<sub>Y</sub> it is 30° + φ, so W<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° − φ) and W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° + φ)
Sum = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ = P; difference = V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> sin φ, so Q = √3(W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub>)
Divide: tan φ = √3(W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub>)/(W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub>)
W<sub>2</sub> = 0 at pf 0.5 (φ = 60°); for a lagging pf below 0.5, cos(30° + φ) < 0 and W<sub>2</sub> reads negative (reverse its voltage coil and count the reading as negative)
answer: Connection: current coils in lines R and Y; voltage coil of W<sub>1</sub> from R to B, of W<sub>2</sub> from Y to B. Each meter reads the average of (its voltage coil voltage) × (its current coil current).

answer.text: Any load, balanced or not (three wires, so i<sub>R</sub> + i<sub>Y</sub> + i<sub>B</sub> = 0 at every instant):
answer.pre:
w<sub>1</sub> + w<sub>2</sub> = v<sub>RB</sub>i<sub>R</sub> + v<sub>YB</sub>i<sub>Y</sub> = (v<sub>R</sub> − v<sub>B</sub>)i<sub>R</sub> + (v<sub>Y</sub> − v<sub>B</sub>)i<sub>Y</sub>
        = v<sub>R</sub>i<sub>R</sub> + v<sub>Y</sub>i<sub>Y</sub> − v<sub>B</sub>(i<sub>R</sub> + i<sub>Y</sub>)
        = v<sub>R</sub>i<sub>R</sub> + v<sub>Y</sub>i<sub>Y</sub> + v<sub>B</sub>i<sub>B</sub>   (since i<sub>R</sub> + i<sub>Y</sub> = −i<sub>B</sub>)

answer: The right side is the total instantaneous power of the load, measured from any common point, star or delta. Averaging both sides: W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> = P. No balance was assumed; only the three-wire condition. In general n wires need n − 1 wattmeters (Blondel's theorem).

Balanced load, R-Y-B sequence, each line current lagging its phase voltage by φ: V<sub>R</sub> = V∠0°, V<sub>Y</sub> = V∠−120°, V<sub>B</sub> = V∠120°. Then V<sub>RB</sub> = V<sub>R</sub> − V<sub>B</sub> = √3V∠−30° and I<sub>R</sub> = I∠−φ, so the angle between them is 30° − φ. V<sub>YB</sub> = V<sub>Y</sub> − V<sub>B</sub> = √3V∠−90° and I<sub>Y</sub> = I∠(−120° − φ), so the angle is 30° + φ.

answer.pre:
W<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° − φ),   W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° + φ)
W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> × 2 cos 30° cos φ = √3 V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos φ = P
W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> × 2 sin 30° sin φ = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> sin φ
tan φ = √3(W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub>)/(W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub>),   Q = √3(W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub>)

answer: Negative reading: W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° + φ) falls to zero at φ = 60° (pf 0.5) and is negative for a lagging pf below 0.5; for a leading load it is W<sub>1</sub> that goes negative. The meter then deflects backwards, so its voltage coil is reversed to get a reading, and the reading is entered with a minus sign in both formulas.
The power-factor formula needs balance: it assumes equal line currents and the same φ in each phase. For an unbalanced load only the sum W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> keeps its meaning.

Check with numbers: W<sub>1</sub> = 5.5 kW, W<sub>2</sub> = 2.5 kW give P = 8.0 kW, tan φ = 1.732 × 3/8 = 0.650, φ = 33.0°, pf 0.839 lagging. Then V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> = 8.0/(√3 × 0.839) = 5.51 kVA and W<sub>1</sub> = 5.51 cos(−3.0°) = 5.50 kW, W<sub>2</sub> = 5.51 cos 63.0° = 2.50 kW.

bank.q: Compare phasor steady-state analysis with the Laplace transform method for an RL circuit switched onto an AC source. When does the transient matter and when can it be ignored?
outline: Phasor method gives only the particular (steady-state) solution; the natural response is deliberately dropped.
Laplace method solves the full differential equation with initial conditions and gives both terms.
For a sine drive the transient decays as e<sup>−t/τ</sup> with τ = L/R; after about 5τ it is below 1% of its initial value.
Transient matters for switching, protection, relay settings, inrush current and short circuits.
Steady state is enough for continuous running equipment, heating, power and power-factor calculations.
Limit of validity: the phasor answer is the Laplace answer as t → ∞.
answer: Take a concrete case: v(t) = 325 sin(314t) V switched at t = 0 onto R = 10 Ω in series with L = 31.8 mH, so X<sub>L</sub> = 10 Ω and τ = L/R = 3.18 ms, with i(0) = 0.

Phasor method: Z = 10 + j10 = 14.14∠45° Ω, so the peak current is 325/14.14 = 22.98 A and i<sub>ss</sub>(t) = 22.98 sin(314t − 45°) A. This is the forced (particular) solution only; it says nothing about how the current starts.

answer.text: Laplace (or classical) method: solve L di/dt + R i = v with i(0) = 0. With V(s) = 325 × 314/(s² + 314²), I(s) = V(s)/(R + sL); partial fractions give the same sinusoid plus one exponential term:
How fast the two answers meet:

answer: After 5τ = 15.9 ms, less than one 20 ms cycle, the transient is e<sup>−5</sup> = 0.7 % of its start. As t → ∞ the Laplace answer becomes the phasor answer exactly, so the phasor method is the Laplace method with the natural response left out.

The size of the transient depends on the switching instant. Closing at a voltage angle α gives K = −22.98 sin(α − 45°): closing at α = 45° gives K = 0 and no transient at all; closing at α = 135° gives the largest offset, K = −22.98 A. Here τ is short, so by the first negative peak at 10 ms the offset has almost gone (−23.97 A against −22.98 A); in a circuit with a large L/R the same offset lasts for many cycles and the first peak approaches twice the steady peak.

When the transient matters: switching and protection studies, inrush current of transformers and motors, fault currents with DC offset that relays and breakers must survive, and circuits with long time constants (large L/R) where it lasts many cycles.

When it can be ignored: equipment that runs continuously, heating, energy metering, power and power-factor calculations, and any question that asks for the steady state. There the phasor method is shorter and gives the same numbers.

bank.q: An unbalanced delta load is connected to a 400 V, three-phase, three-wire, R-Y-B supply: Z<sub>RY</sub> = 20 Ω, Z<sub>YB</sub> = 10 + j10 Ω, Z<sub>BR</sub> = 16 − j12 Ω. Find the phase and line currents and the total power. Two wattmeters have their current coils in R and Y and their voltage coils to B: find their readings, and show whether the two-wattmeter power-factor formula can be used here.
outline: Take V<sub>RY</sub> = 400∠0°, V<sub>YB</sub> = 400∠−120°, V<sub>BR</sub> = 400∠120°
Phase currents I<sub>RY</sub> = 20∠0°, I<sub>YB</sub> = 28.28∠−165°, I<sub>BR</sub> = 20∠156.87° A
Line currents by KCL: I<sub>R</sub> = I<sub>RY</sub> − I<sub>BR</sub> = 39.19∠−11.57°, I<sub>Y</sub> = 47.88∠−171.21°, I<sub>B</sub> = 17.61∠59.53° A; they sum to zero
W<sub>1</sub> = 10.4 kW, W<sub>2</sub> = 12.0 kW; W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> = 22.4 kW equals P
The power-factor formula gives a leading angle, but the load is lagging: it is valid only for a balanced load
answer: In a delta each branch sits across one line voltage, which the supply fixes. Take V<sub>RY</sub> = 400∠0°, V<sub>YB</sub> = 400∠−120°, V<sub>BR</sub> = 400∠120° V.

answer.text: Line currents by KCL at the three corners of the delta:

answer: Check: the real parts 38.39 − 47.32 + 8.93 = 0 and the imaginary parts −7.86 − 7.32 + 15.18 = 0, so I<sub>R</sub> + I<sub>Y</sub> + I<sub>B</sub> = 0, as it must with three wires. The line currents are unequal and not 120° apart, and none of them is √3 times a phase current.

answer.text: Wattmeter readings, W = |V||I| cos(angle between them):

answer: Sum: W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> = 10.40 + 12.00 = 22.40 kW, exactly the total found branch by branch. The sum works for an unbalanced load.

The power-factor formula would give tan φ = √3(10.40 − 12.00)/22.40 = −0.124, a leading angle of 7.0°. The load is in fact lagging, with Q/P = 3200/22 400 = 0.143 (an overall angle of 8.1°). The formula assumes equal line currents and one φ for all phases, so for an unbalanced load it gives a wrong answer: only the sum is trustworthy.

bank.q: An industrial consumer runs at 0.7 power factor lagging and is charged a penalty. Explain the causes and effects of low power factor, and calculate the capacitor kvar needed to raise it to 0.95 for a 100 kW load.
outline: Causes: induction motors running light, transformers on part load, arc furnaces, welding sets.
Effects: larger current for the same kW, bigger cables and switchgear, more I²R losses and voltage drop, higher tariff.
Initial: φ₁ = cos⁻¹0.7 = 45.6°, Q₁ = 100 tan 45.6° = 102 kvar.
Target: φ₂ = cos⁻¹0.95 = 18.2°, Q₂ = 100 tan 18.2° = 32.9 kvar.
Capacitor rating = Q₁ − Q₂ ≈ 69 kvar; P stays at 100 kW throughout.
Capacitors supply the reactive power locally, so the line current and losses fall while kW is unchanged; warn about over-correction leading to leading pf and resonance with supply harmonics.
answer: Causes of low power factor: induction motors, which need magnetising current and run at very low pf when lightly loaded; transformers on light load; arc furnaces, welding sets and fluorescent chokes. All draw a large lagging reactive current.

Effects: for the same kW the current rises as 1/pf, so cables, transformers and switchgear must be larger, I²R losses and voltage drop rise, generators deliver fewer kW for their kVA rating, and the supply tariff adds a penalty for low pf (the exact rule depends on the tariff).

answer.text: Reactive power before and after, with P = 100 kW unchanged:

answer: Capacitor rating: Q<sub>C</sub> = Q<sub>1</sub> − Q<sub>2</sub> = P(tan φ<sub>1</sub> − tan φ<sub>2</sub>) = 100 × (1.020 − 0.329) = 69.2 kvar, connected in parallel with the load.

Effect on current, taking a 415 V three-phase supply: I = P/(√3 × 415 × pf). Before: 100 000/(1.732 × 415 × 0.70) = 198.7 A. After: 100 000/(1.732 × 415 × 0.95) = 146.4 A, a fall of 26 %. Line losses go as I², so they fall to (146.4/198.7)² = 0.54 of their old value.
Size of a delta-connected bank on 415 V: each phase supplies 69.2/3 = 23.05 kvar across 415 V, so C = Q/(ωV²) = 23 050/(314.16 × 415²) = 426 µF per phase.

Why 0.95 and not 1.0: raising pf to 1.0 needs the full 102 kvar for a further cut in current of only 5 % (146.4 A to 139.1 A), and when the motor load drops the fixed bank over-corrects to a leading pf and raises the voltage. Banks are therefore switched in steps.

A caution from non-sinusoidal waveforms: a capacitor bank and the supply inductance can resonate at a harmonic frequency, so plants with rectifiers or drives use detuned banks (a series reactor with each capacitor).
Check: after correction S = 100 + j(102.0 − 69.2) = 100 + j32.9 kVA, |S| = 105.3 kVA and pf = 100/105.3 = 0.95.

glossary.def: A quantity that varies as the sine of an angle, written v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ).
The peak value V<sub>m</sub> of a sinusoid, measured from zero to crest.
The time T = 1/f for one complete cycle, in seconds.
ω = 2πf, the rate of change of the angle in rad/s.
The angle φ that fixes where the waveform starts at t = 0, in degrees or radians.
The square root of the mean of the squared waveform over one period; the equivalent DC heating value.
The area under one half cycle divided by the half period; 0.637 V<sub>m</sub> for a sine.
RMS value divided by average value; 1.11 for a pure sine.
A complex number representing the amplitude and phase of a sinusoid at a fixed frequency.
The complex ratio V/I, written R + jX, measured in ohms.
The imaginary part of impedance; ωL for an inductor, −1/(ωC) for a capacitor.
The reciprocal of impedance, Y = G + jB, measured in siemens.
The condition ωL = 1/(ωC) at which the net reactance is zero and current is limited only by resistance.
The average power actually converted to work or heat, P = VI cos φ, in watts.
The power that oscillates between source and reactance with zero net transfer, Q = VI sin φ, in var.
The product of RMS voltage and RMS current, |S| = VI, in volt-amperes.
S = V I* = P + jQ, a single complex number holding both real and reactive power.
The cosine of the angle between voltage and current; also real power divided by apparent power.
A right triangle with P, Q and S as its sides, showing how the three powers relate.
The order in which the three phase voltages of a supply reach their maximum values.
The voltage measured between any two lines of a three-phase system.
The fourth conductor of a star system that carries the unbalanced current back to the source.
A sinusoidal component whose frequency is an integer multiple of the fundamental.
The RMS value of all harmonics above the fundamental, expressed as a fraction of the fundamental RMS.
